text.p: These are the leading stories in Serbian and Montenegrin press on Monday. Reuters has not verified them nor does it vouch for their accuracy.
- S E R B I A -
NASA BORBA
- Strike of employees in the health and social security sectors enters third week.
- Sacked customs officials and people dissatisfied over treatment by customs officials on borders to organise protest outside Federal Customs Administration on June 15.
- Zoran Djindjic re-elected party president at Democratic Party's fifth regular annual assembly.
- Montenegrin government says emphasizing north-south region differences in the republic sensitive and detrimental.
- Yugoslav President Zoran Lilic's mandate expires in one minth, new federation president to be elected by July 25, parliament experts say.
- Macedonian President Kiro Gligorov says fate of Serbia's province Kosovo will depend on its majority Albanian population.
- Bosnian Serb parliament to discuss implementation of agreement on special and parallel ties between Bosnian Serb Republic and Yugoslavia.
- Why is production in Yugoslavia, "a state with the highest growth rate in Europe," as the Serbian president describes it, stagnating, Nasa Borba asks in a commentary.
- Around 22,000 teachers in 242 schools throughout Serbia begin strike over delays in wages.
- Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and his wife Mira Markovic attend opening of their son Marko's discotheque Madonna in Pozarevac.
POLITIKA
- Serbian Interior Ministry says cars with license plates from Bosnian Serb Republic and Eastern Slavonia region in Croatia can be registered in Serbia if they have papers on origin and ownership.
- Is solution in sight for holders of frozen old hard currency savings accounts? Final repayment of 6.5 billion German marks debt to depositors not later than the year 2010.
- So far 4,000 eyewitness statements obtained; The Hague war crimes tirbunal does not treat all sides equally, says Yugoslav committee for gathering information on war crimes.
- Threats and attacks on judges in Yugoslavia increasing.
BORBA
- U.S.-Yugoslav Business Council meeting in New York this week to promote bilateral economic ties.

- Large investment projects will be difficult to carry out without foreign capital and concessions are one of the means to attract capital, says Serbian power company EPS board of directors chairman Dragan Kostic.
- Total value of Yugoslav construction firms' works in the Commonwealth of Independent States expected to reach $600 million in 1997.

- Not everything can be privatised. Socially owned capital of public enterprises cannot be tranformed into private property either through sale of existing or issue of new shares, says Federal Constitutional Court.
VECERNJE NOVOSTI

- The country ruled by Josip Broz Tito was attractive, there was freedom of movement and life was good, Sarajevo daily Oslobodjenje writes on the occasion of the 105th birthday of the late Yugoslav leader.
- "I am not afraid of being caught. I would go to The Hague if it were not discriminatory and biased," says former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
- M O N T E N E G R O -
POBJEDA

- Minister of Culture Goran Rakocevic opened refurbished Montenegrin theatre building. Opening ceremony attended by republican parliament speaker Svetozar Marovic, prime minister Milo Djukanovic and representatives of the federal state, the republic of Serbia and the diplomatic corps. No mention of Montenegrin President Momir Bulatovic attending.
- Montenegrin minister of police Filip Vujanovic denied allegations in president Bulatovic's interview that Montenegrin police worked irresponsibly.
- Niksic will get 1,024 new telephone lines by opening new switchboards in Rubezi and Ozrnici. There are some 16,000 telephone connections in Niksic. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
